title: Displacement-field-driven reconstruction of low energy transport in few-layer PtSe2
authors: Xiao Liu, Yaroslav Zhumagulov, Yuang Jie, Ahmet Enes Bozcali, Johan Felisaz, Qi Zhang, Oldvrich Cicvarek, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Zdeněk Sofer, Oleg V. Yazyev, Ahmet Avsar
abstract: In layered semiconductors, a perpendicular displacement field generates an interlayer potential difference that competes with interlayer hybridization, modifying both the band gap and the finite-density electronic states that carry current. Resolving this interplay requires a material lying close to the semiconductor-to-semimetal transition, where moderate electric fields can strongly reshape the low-energy electronic structure. Here, we investigate displacement-field-driven transport in dual-gated semiconducting PtSe2, whose pronounced thickness-dependent electronic structure provides access to this low-band-gap regime. Unlike thinner layers, the displacement-field response is strong in six-layer PtSe2, which lies at the verge of the semiconductor-to-semimetal crossover with only a small residual transport gap. Even weak displacement fields rapidly suppress this residual gap near charge neutrality, driving the system toward a band-overlap regime. At the same time, the conductivity decreases in the heavily hole-doped regime, demonstrating that the displacement field modifies not only the gap but also the conducting valence-band states. Fixed-relaxation-time Wannier transport calculations reproduce both responses, showing that they originate from field-induced band overlap together with reconstruction of the valence-band dispersion. These results establish finite-density transport as a sensitive probe of displacement-field-driven electronic structure reconstruction and extend electrical control beyond conventional band-gap engineering.
summary: This work demonstrates that applying an external perpendicular electric field can fundamentally reconstruct the electronic band structure in few-layer PtSe2, particularly when the material is near a semiconductor-to-semimetal transition. By measuring transport properties, the authors show that this field causes gap closure and modifies valence-band conductivity. This establishes finite-density transport as a sensitive tool for probing field-driven electronic structure engineering beyond simple band-gap control.
main_problem: The study investigates how a perpendicular displacement field modifies the low-energy electronic transport in few-layer semiconductors, focusing on the interplay between the field and interlayer hybridization.
main_result: The displacement field strongly reconstructs the low-energy band structure, causing gap suppression near charge neutrality and modifying valence-band conductivity in a thickness-dependent manner.
method: The research combines electrical transport measurements on dual-gated devices with theoretical modeling using Wannier tight-binding calculations.
model_or_system: The system is few-layer PtSe2, a layered semiconductor whose electronic structure is sensitive to thickness. The theoretical model uses a Wannier Hamiltonian incorporating an out-of-plane electric field term.
key_observables: Conductance (G), minimum current, normalized current vs. displacement field (D), and the evolution of the band gap.
important_parameters: Layer thickness (3L vs 6L), temperature (50 K to 300 K), and the magnitude of the perpendicular electric field (D).
main_assumptions: The theoretical calculations utilize a fixed-relaxation-time approximation and neglect contact resistance or field-dependent disorder scattering.
figures_summary: Figures show device structures, temperature-dependent transfer/output characteristics, current maps, and theoretical conductance plots confirming field-induced band overlap and reconstruction.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the physical setup using device measurements, presents the core findings regarding field-induced transport changes in 6L PtSe2, and supports these observations with detailed Wannier model calculations.
why_interesting: While focused on solid-state physics, the concept of external fields inducing fundamental changes in electronic band structure and transport properties is relevant to understanding engineered quantum materials and open quantum systems.
